title: Bookland, the country on every book
hook: The barcode on the back of a book says it was made in a country that does not exist.
peek: Most book barcodes begin with 978. In the retail barcode system, the first digits usually name a country, and 978 belongs to Bookland, an imaginary country created so that every book's ISBN could double as a shop barcode.
lede: Shop barcodes in the international EAN system start with a prefix that usually points to a country, such as 50 for the United Kingdom. Books needed a way into that system without new numbers, so the codes 978 and later 979 were set aside for a made-up country called Bookland. Put 978 in front of an old ISBN and it becomes a barcode.

bullets.text: The idea began in Britain in the mid-1960s, when the bookseller W H Smith wanted to computerise its stock. A nine-digit Standard Book Numbering scheme followed, and in 1970 it became the international ISBN, with ten digits.
The last digit of a ten-digit ISBN is a check, worked out from the others to catch typing mistakes. Because the sum can need the value 10, some ISBNs end in the Roman numeral X.
Since 1 January 2007, ISBNs have been 13 digits long, exactly matching the barcode. Publishers were running short of numbers, so Bookland's second prefix, 979, came into use alongside 978.
Bookland exists because books had to scan at the same tills as groceries. The bars under a book's ISBN are the same kind of code that first beeped through a supermarket checkout in 1974.
